snip.t: Bronchiectasis is permanent, abnormal dilatation of the bronchi with chronic inflammation and infection, leading to a clinical syndrome of chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections and sometimes haemoptysis.

Bronchial arterial supply – systemic bronchial arteries run alongside bronchi: Chronic inflammation induces neovascularisation; fragile bronchial vessels are the source of haemoptysis when they rupture.
PE (Wells): clinical signs of DVT · PE is the most likely diagnosis · HR above 100 · immobilisation or surgery in the last 4 weeks · previous DVT or PE · haemoptysis · malignancy.
snip.s: DVT and Venous Thromboembolism (with Pulmonary Embolism)

snip.t: Return if breathless, high fever, cough over 3 weeks, haemoptysis, weight loss, or HIV (consider pneumonia or TB).
Neovascularisation of granulation tissue → Potential haemorrhage → haemoptysis
Insidious or subacute: fever, night sweats, cough with large volumes of purulent and often foul-smelling sputum (suggests anaerobes), weight loss, malaise, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis.

Lung cancer: Carcinogenic dust (silica, asbestos, diesel) + chronic inflammation — New infiltrate, weight loss, haemoptysis; prognosis poorer than idiopathic lung cancer — 15–30 yr latency; risk proportional to cumulative exposure
PE: sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, haemoptysis, tachycardia, tachypnoea, fever (low grade), syncope; massive PE: hypotension, shock, cyanosis, raised JVP, cardiac arrest.
snip.s: DVT and Venous Thromboembolism (with Pulmonary Embolism)

qs.q: A 45-year-old man has a 3-month history of recurrent sinusitis, epistaxis, haemoptysis, and haematuria. CXR shows bilateral cavitating nodules. Urinalysis shows red cell casts. c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) is strongly positive. Most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: This is a classic presentation of Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA), formerly Wegener's granulomatosis. It is a small vessel vasculitis characterized by necrotizing granulomas involving the upper and lower respiratory tracts, glomerulonephritis, and is strongly associated with c-ANCA (antibodies against proteinase 3, PR3-ANCA).
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 24-year-old male smoker presents with haemoptysis and progressive dyspnea. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and red cell casts. CXR reveals bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Anti-GBM antibodies are strongly positive. Renal biopsy shows linear IgG deposits along the glomerular basement membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: The presence of haemoptysis, renal disease with red cell casts, positive anti-GBM antibodies, and linear IgG deposition on renal biopsy is pathognomonic for Anti-GBM Disease, also known as Goodpasture Syndrome when pulmonary and renal involvement are present.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 9, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 62-year-old male smoker presents with a central hilar mass and haemoptysis. Biopsy shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. Which paraneoplastic syndrome is most expected?
o: Cushing syndrome resulting from ectopic ACTH production by the tumour
Hypercalcaemia resulting from parathyroid hormone-related peptide secretion
Lambert-Eaton syndrome resulting from calcium channel antibody production
SIADH causing severe hyponatraemia and concentrated urine output
qs.e: Squamous cell carcinoma secretes PTH-related peptide causing humoral hypercalcaemia — the most characteristic paraneoplastic syndrome of squamous cell carcinoma.
